messages.author: 3c35c7ccb6bfb7dd
messages.subject: offset slow down the sampler?
parts:
Hi,

I am fitting a negative binomial glm as the following:

Y_{k,i} ~ NB(phi, phi / mu_k )

log(mu_k) = X_k \beta

As you see, my data is clustered and I am not modeling any random
effects, yet. This works well.

But when I include an offset to mu_k:

log(mu_k) = offset_k + X_k \beta

Stan works a lot slower compared to the one without offset. I am not
familiar with HMC so I'd appreciated if any one could point out the
reason. And, is there any ways to speed up ?

I put the stan code (for the one with offset) here:

data {
int N;
int k;
int cuts[N];
int counts[N];
int index[N];
vector[k] offset;
}

parameters {
real<lower=0> phi;
vector[k] beta;
}

model {

vector[N] logliks;

phi ~ gamma(2, 0.5);
for(i in 1:k) {
beta[i] ~ normal(0,1);
}

for(i in 1:N) {
logliks[i] <- counts[i] * neg_binomial_log(cuts[i], phi, phi /
(offset[index[i]] * exp(beta[index[i]])));
}
lp__ <- lp__ + sum(logliks);
}

Thanks a lot!

Jianling

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: offset slow down the sampler?
parts:
On Wednesday, December 26, 2012 12:26:06 PM UTC-5, Jianling wrote:
Hi,

I am fitting a negative binomial glm as the following:

Y_{k,i} ~ NB(phi, phi / mu_k )

log(mu_k) = X_k \beta

As you see, my data is clustered and I am not modeling any random
effects, yet. This works well.

But when I include an offset to mu_k:

log(mu_k) = offset_k + X_k \beta

Stan works a lot slower compared to the one without offset. I am not
familiar with HMC so I'd appreciated if any one could point out the
reason. And, is there any ways to speed up ?

I am surprised that simply including an offset would make a noticeable difference in the speed the evaluate the log-posterior. I would guess that it is increasing the rejection rate of proposals, perhaps due to overflow. In general, with GLM's it is often good to write some custom code for a few reasons. First, you can use whatever parameterization of the distribution you want, rather than the one(s) that come with Stan. Second, you can avoid some round-tripping of transformations that may introduce overflow or underflow. We've done so already with variants of the bernoulli and Poisson distributions, but not yet for the negative binomial, beta, etc.

It sounds like you might prefer the parameterization of the negative binomial in terms of the mean and dispersion, rather than the parameterization in Stan which utilizes a shape and an inverse scale parameter. If so, let me know and I'll work through the math / Stan code.

One simple thing that can be done is to vectorize the prior, rather than looping, i.e. do

beta ~ normal(0,1);

Ben

Thanks, Ben. 

When you say writing some custom code, do you mean code just for calculating the pmf or do you mean stan itself isn't suitable for this task yet? I wrote some mcmc R code before and the mixing isn't working well, that's why I tried stan and it seems working great, except for the slow speed in some cases.

Maybe I can try to write the beta and negative binomial pmf myself in the stan model definition and see how it works. 

As for the parameterization for the pmf, any form is fine, unless transforming the parameters takes a lot time ( which I assume doesn't ). I do have a suggesting, though:  the pmf's in stan can take vectors as parameters, but it internally sums up the log densities. Wouldn't it be easier to work with if it returns a vector, instead of returning a summation. Another related, is it possible to add a 'count' parameter to the pmf functions? Then instead of calculating the log pmf for the same value multiple times,  it can just be calculated once and then multiplied by the 'count'.

Thanks.

Jianling

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: offset slow down the sampler? (negative binomial speed)
parts:
On 12/26/12 3:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Wednesday, December 26, 2012 12:26:06 PM UTC-5, Jianling wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I am fitting a negative binomial glm as the following:
>
> Y_{k,i} ~ NB(phi, phi / mu_k )
>
> log(mu_k) = X_k \beta

This requires:

mu_k <- exp(X_k * beta);

inv_scale <- phi / mu_k;

This may be more arithmetically stable if you
implement it as:

inv_scale <- exp(log(phi) - mu_k);

> As you see, my data is clustered and I am not modeling any random
> effects, yet. This works well.
>
> But when I include an offset to mu_k:
>
> log(mu_k) = offset_k + X_k \beta
>
> Stan works a lot slower compared to the one without offset. I am not
> familiar with HMC so I'd appreciated if any one could point out the
> reason. And, is there any ways to speed up ?

The speed and stability for negative binomial will improve in our
next release. We need to vectorize the gradient calcs and make
some of our own internal calcs more stable. Right now, we evaluate

log ( inv_scale / (1 - inv_scale) )

which would most likely be problematic in cases where inv_scale
is close to 0 or close to 1. This should also be evaluated as:

log(inv_scale) - log1m(inv_scale),

which should be much more arithmetically stable for inv_scale near
1 and somewhat more stable for inv_scale near 0.

We're also working on adding alternative parameterizations.

Vectorizing the negative binomial won't make things much faster
at the moment because the gradients aren't vectorized internally.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: offset slow down the sampler?
parts:
On 12/26/12 5:00 PM, Jianling Zhong wrote:
> Thanks, Ben.
>
> When you say writing some custom code, do you mean code just for calculating the pmf or do you mean stan itself isn't
> suitable for this task yet? I wrote some mcmc R code before and the mixing isn't working well, that's why I tried stan
> and it seems working great, except for the slow speed in some cases.

> Maybe I can try to write the beta and negative binomial pmf myself in the stan model definition and see how it works.

You can always unfold directly and increment lp__ with
the log probabilities.

As we optimize more and more of the probability functions (we
first vectorized them so the language wouldn't change so much,
but we're going through and unfolding the gradient calcs and
doing algebra to reduce repeated computations with vectorization),
you shouldn't need to do this.

> As for the parameterization for the pmf, any form is fine, unless transforming the parameters takes a lot time ( which I
> assume doesn't ). I do have a suggesting, though: the pmf's in stan can take vectors as parameters, but it internally

> sums up the log densities.Wouldn't it be easier to work with if it returns a vector, instead of returning a summation.

The reason it returns a single value is that we need to return a single
log probabilty in the end. By taking the entire summation as a single
value, we can make the auto-dif more efficient.

Also, it doesn't compute them independently. It will share
computations that only need to be done once. That is, the
individual log densities often aren't even computed directly.
See the example of log(sigma) below.

> Another related, is it possible to add a 'count' parameter to the pmf functions? Then instead of calculating the log pmf
> for the same value multiple times, it can just be calculated once and then multiplied by the 'count'.

We don't have any plans to add count features like this (other
than the obvious binomial and multinomial counting up bernoulli
and categorical pmfs).

The probability functions we've optimized already do this internally
for parameters if there are scalar parameters mixed with vector parameters.
So if you have

y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

and y is a vector and sigma is a scalar, Stan will only
compute log(sigma) once.

But if you really just want to count the same data point y with the
same parameters mu and sigma a a total of N times, you can do, for instance

for (n in 1:N)
y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

but it's more efficient to just do as you suggest
and multiply because we're on the log scale:

lp__ <- lp__ + N * normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

- Bob
